nodes.name: Nakayama corollary: basis of M/mM generates M
nodes.statement: Let $(R,\mathfrak{m},k)$ be a local ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. If the elements $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ are elements in $M$ that form a basis in the projection $M / \mathfrak{m} M$, then $x_1, ldots, x_n$ generate $M$.

nodes.name: projective resolution
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring. Let $M$ be an $R$-module. A projective resolution of $M$ over $R$ Is an exact sequence \[ \ldots \to P^2 \to P^1 \to P^0 \to M \to 0 \]. That is to say, a projective resolution is a quasi-isomorphism of complexes between the inclusion of $M$ into chain complexes over $R$ (i.e. the complex which has $M$ in degree zero, trivial everywhere else, with trivial maps) and a bounded—below complex whose components are projective $R$-modules.
nodes.statement_short: An exact sequence of projectives $\ldots\to P^1\to P^0\to M\to 0$, i.e. a quasi-isomorphism from a bounded-below projective complex to $M$.
nodes.label: def:projv_resl

nodes.name: free resolution
nodes.statement: A free resolution of $M$ over $R$ is a projective resolution whose components $P^i$ are free.
nodes.label: def:free_resl

nodes.name: length of a projective resolution
nodes.statement: The length of a projective resolution $P_\cdot$ is the highest $i$ such that $P^i$ is nonzero. If there exists no such $i$, the length is infinity
nodes.label: def:length_of_resl

nodes.name: projective dimension
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Then $\projdim M$ is the minimum length of a projective resolution of $M$. It lives in the set $\mathbb{N} \cap \infty$.
nodes.label: def:projdim

nodes.name: Finite resolution implies finite projective dimension

conclusions: $\projdim M < \infty$
nodes.label: lem:finite_resl_implies_finite_projdim

nodes.name: Prime Avoidance
nodes.statement: (See BH 1.2.2) Let \(R\) be a ring, and \(\mathfrak{p}_{1}, \ldots, \mathfrak{p}_{m}\) be prime ideals. Let \(M\) be an \(R\)-module, and let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} \in M\). Let \(N\) be the submodule generated by \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\). If \(N_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}} \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}M_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}}\) for all \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\), then there exist \(a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \in R\) such that \(x_{1} + \sum_{i=2}^{n} a_{i}x_{i} \not\in \mathfrak{p}_{j} M_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}} \) for all \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\).
assumptions: Let \(R\) be a ring, and \(\mathfrak{p}_{1}, \ldots, \mathfrak{p}_{m}\) be prime ideals.
Let \(M\) be an \(R\)-module, and let \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n} \in M\).
Let \(N\) be the submodule generated by \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n}\).
\(N_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}} \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}M_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}}\) for all \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\)
conclusions: there exist \(a_{2}, \ldots, a_{n} \in R\) such that \(x_{1} + \sum_{i=2}^{n} a_{i}x_{i} \not\in \mathfrak{p}_{j} M_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}} \) for all \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\)
nodes.statement_short: Module version of prime avoidance: if $N$ is not locally inside $\mathfrak{p}_jM$ for each $j$, some combination $x_1+\sum a_ix_i$ avoids all of them.
nodes.label: lem:prime_avoidance

nodes.name: Prime Avoidance for rings
nodes.statement: Let \(R\) be a ring, and \(\mathfrak{p}_{1}, \ldots, \mathfrak{p}_{m}\) be prime ideals. Let \(I\) be a finitely generated ideal of \(R\). Then if \(I \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}\) for all \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\), then there exists an \(x \in I\) such that \(x \not\in \mathfrak{p}_{j}\) for all \(j\).
assumptions: Let \(R\) be a ring, and \(\mathfrak{p}_{1}, \ldots, \mathfrak{p}_{m}\) be prime ideals.
Let \(I\) be a finitely generated ideal of \(R\).
\(I \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}\) for all \(j \in \{1, \ldots, m\}\)

nodes.name: Proof of Prime Avoidance for rings
nodes.statement: Take \(M = R\) in the previous theorem. Using the correspondence theorem for localizations, the condition \(I_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}} \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}R_{\mathfrak{p}_{j}}\) is the same as \(I \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}\).

assumptions: Let \(E\) be an additive subgroup of \(R\) which is multiplicatively closed.
Let \(I_{1}, \ldots, I_{n}\) be ideals such that \(I_{3}, \ldots, I_{n}\) are prime.
\(E\) is not contained in any one of the \(I_{j}\)
conclusions: \(E\) is not contained in their union

If \(I \not\subset \mathfrak{p}_{j}\) for all \(j\), then there exists some \(y \in J\) such that \(x + y \not\in \mathfrak{p}_{j}\) for all \(j\)

nodes.name: height of a prime ideal
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring, and $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal in $R$.- Then the height of $\mathfrak{p}$ is the sup of the lengths of chains \[ \mathfrak{p} = \mathfrak{p}_0 \supset \mathfrak{p}_1 \supset \dots \supset \mathfrak{p}_n . \]
nodes.statement_short: Height of a prime is the sup of lengths of descending prime chains starting at it.
nodes.label: def:Ideal.primeHeight

nodes.name: height of an ideal
nodes.statement: The height of an ideal \(I \subset R\) is the infimum of the heights of prime ideals containing \(I\).
nodes.genus: infimum of the heights of prime ideals containing \(I\)
nodes.label: def:Ideal.height

nodes.name: Height of a prime ideal agrees with height as an ideal
nodes.statement: Sanity lemma: this definition of height agrees with the previous when \(I\) is prime (all by def).
nodes.statement_short: For a prime ideal, the ideal height coincides with the prime height, by definition.

nodes.name: Krull dimension
nodes.statement: The Krull dimension of the \(R\) is the supremum of heights of prime ideals \(\mathfrak{p} \subset R\).
nodes.label: def:krull_dim_ring

nodes.name: Dimension of a localization equals height
nodes.statement: Let \(R\) a ring and \(\mathfrak{p}\) a prime ideal, then \[ \dim R_{\mathfrak{p}} = \height \mathfrak{p} \]
assumptions: Let \(R\) a ring and \(\mathfrak{p}\) a prime ideal
conclusions: \[ \dim R_{\mathfrak{p}} = \height \mathfrak{p} \]
nodes.label: lem:dim_local_eq_height_prime

nodes.name: Proof that dim of localization is height
nodes.statement: This is a ``straightforward'' application of the correspondance theorem for localizations.
nodes.statement_short: Correspondence theorem for localizations.

nodes.name: Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem
nodes.statement: Let \(R\) be a noetherian ring, and \(I\) a prinicpal ideal. Then each minimal prime ideal over \(I\) (i.e. minimal among primes containing I) has height at most 1.
assumptions: Let \(R\) be a noetherian ring, and \(I\) a prinicpal ideal.
conclusions: Then each minimal prime ideal over \(I\) (i.e. minimal among primes containing I) has height at most 1.
nodes.label: thm:krull_principal_ideal

nodes.name: Proof of Krull's Principal Ideal Theorem
nodes.statement: See the Wikipedia page about Krull's principal ideal theorem (recieved June 27 2023) for a detailed proof, it uses passing to the quotient and the definition of Artinian rings.
nodes.statement_short: Pointer to Wikipedia: pass to a quotient and use Artinian rings.

nodes.name: Krull's Height Theorem
nodes.statement: Let \(I = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})\) be an ideal. Then each minimal prime over \(I\) has height at most \(n\).
assumptions: Let \(I = (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{n})\) be an ideal.
conclusions: Then each minimal prime over \(I\) has height at most \(n\).
nodes.label: thm:krull_height

nodes.name: Proof of Krull's Height Theorem
nodes.statement: Use Krull's prinipal ideal and induct on the number of elements, see Wikipedia for details.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of generators using the principal ideal theorem.

nodes.name: Converse of Krull's Height Theorem
nodes.statement: Let \(R\) a noetherian ring, and \(I\) a proper ideal of height \(n\). Then for all \(1 \leq i \leq n\), there exist elements \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i}\) such that \(\height (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i}) = i\).
assumptions: Let \(R\) a noetherian ring, and \(I\) a proper ideal of height \(n\).
conclusions: Then for all \(1 \leq i \leq n\), there exist elements \(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i}\) such that \(\height (x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i}) = i\).
nodes.label: thm:genset_of_any_height_of_noetherian_height_n

nodes.name: Proof of the converse of Krull's Height Theorem
nodes.statement: We will successively apply prime avoidance. Base case: \(I\) is not contained in any minimal prime of \(R\), otherwise \(I\) would have height zero (if I had height zero, we're already done). By prime avoidance, we can pick an element \(x_{1}\) which is not in any minimal prime. Thus, any prime containing \(x_{1}\) must also contain a minimal prime, so all such primes have height at least 1. Pick a prime which is minimal among those containing \((x_{1})\) (equivalently, pick one which is minimal in the ring \(R / (x_{1})\)). By the above discussion, it must have height at least one. By Krull's principal ideal/height theorem, it must have at most height 1, and we conclude it has height 1. Inductive step: Copy-paste the previous discussion, with "zero" replaced by "\(n-1\)", "1" replaced by "\(n\)", and "minimal prime of \(R\) " replaced by "minimal prime containing \((x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i-1})\)", "\(x_{1}\)" replaced by "\(x_{i}\)", and "\((x_{1})\) replaced by \((x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i})\)".
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $i$ by successive prime avoidance. Each new element avoids the minimal primes, and Krull's theorem caps the height.

nodes.name: Dimension Theorem
nodes.statement: Let \((R,\mathfrak{m},k)\) be a local noetherian ring. Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). Then the following are equivalent \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] \(\dim R = n\) \item[(b)] \(\height \mathfrak{m} = n\) \item[(c)] \(\nu(R) = n\) \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let \((R,\mathfrak{m},k)\) be a local noetherian ring.
Let \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).
conclusions: the following are equivalent \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] \(\dim R = n\) \item[(b)] \(\height \mathfrak{m} = n\) \item[(c)] \(\nu(R) = n\) \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For a local noetherian ring, Krull dimension, height of $\mathfrak{m}$ and system-of-parameters length $\nu(R)$ coincide.
nodes.label: thm:dimension_theorem

nodes.name: Proof of the Dimension Theorem
nodes.statement: The equivalence of (a) and (b) is Lemma \ref{lem:dim_local_eq_height_prime} applied to the situation of a local ring. The directions of (b) \(\iff\) (c) are given by Theorems \ref{thm:krull_height} and \ref{thm:genset_of_any_height_of_noetherian_height_n}, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: (a)<=>(b) by localization lemma; (b)<=>(c) by Krull's height theorem and its converse.

nodes.name: Quotient by a regular element drops dimension
nodes.statement: Let \(R\) be a ring, and \(M\) an \(R\)-module. Let \(x\) be an \(M\)-regular element. Then \(\dim M / xM \leq \dim M - 1\).
assumptions: Let \(R\) be a ring, and \(M\) an \(R\)-module.
Let \(x\) be an \(M\)-regular element.
conclusions: Then \(\dim M / xM \leq \dim M - 1\).
nodes.label: thm:quotient_regular_sub_dim_1

nodes.name: Proof that a regular element drops dimension
nodes.statement: As \(x\) is \(M\)-regular, we have that \(x \notin \mathfrak{p}\) for all \(p \in \operatorname{Assoc} M\), otherwise there would be \(M\)-torsion. By definition, \(\dim M = \dim R / \operatorname{Ann} M\). The associated primes of \(M\) are the same as the minimal primes in \(R / \operatorname{Ann} M\), so \(x\) is not contained in any such prime. But then, any chain of prime ideals in \((R / \operatorname{Ann} M) / (x)\) lifts to a chain in \(R / \operatorname{Ann} M\) of ideals which contain \((x)\). But then the smallest ideal in the chain is not minimal since it contains \(x\), so we can extend it to a minimal prime.
nodes.statement_short: A regular element avoids associated (= minimal) primes of $R/\operatorname{Ann}M$, so prime chains in the quotient extend by one.

nodes.name: Quotient by a non-minimal element drops dimension
nodes.statement: Let $x \in R$ be an element which is not in any minimal prime ideal. Then $\dim R / (x) \leq \dim R - 1$
assumptions: Let $x \in R$ be an element which is not in any minimal prime ideal.
conclusions: Then $\dim R / (x) \leq \dim R - 1$
nodes.label: cor:quotient_non_minimal_sub_dim_1

nodes.name: Proof of the dimension-drop corollary
nodes.statement: Take $M = R$ in the previous theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the previous theorem to $M=R$.

nodes.name: M-regular element
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module. An element $x \in R$ is $M$-regular if it does not annihilate any element in $M$. In colon notation, it is non a member of the ideal $( 0 : M )$. If $x$ is an $R$-regular element, we simply say it is a regular element.
differentia: does not annihilate any element in $M$
nodes.label: def:reg_elt

nodes.name: weak M-regular sequence
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module. Then a weak $M$-regular sequence is a sequence $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ with $x_i \in R$ for all $i$, such that $x_i$ is a $M / (x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}) M$-regular element for all $i$. If $M = R$, we say that $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ is a weak regular sequence.
nodes.genus: sequence $x_1, \ldots, x_n$ with $x_i \in R$ for all $i$
differentia: $x_i$ is a $M / (x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}) M$-regular element for all $i$
nodes.label: def:weak_reg_seq

nodes.name: M-regular sequence
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module. An $M$-regular sequence is a weak $M$-regular sequence such that $M / (x_1, \ldots, x_n) M \neq 0$, that is $IM \neq M$. If $M = R$, we simply call this a regular sequence.
nodes.label: def:reg_seq

nodes.name: regular local ring
nodes.statement: A local ring $R$ is regular if $\mathfrak{m}$ is generated by a system of parameters.
differentia: $\mathfrak{m}$ is generated by a system of parameters
nodes.label: def:reg_loc

equivalent_conditions: the minimal number of generators of its maximal ideal is equal to the (Krull) dimension of \(R\)

nodes.name: Proof of BH 2.2.5
nodes.statement: See Bruns-Herzog 2.2.5. This uses BH 2.2.4 (which is Proposition \ref{prop:reg_quot_sys_param}) for the forward direction, and for the reverse direction, we use BH 1.2.12 (aka Theorem \ref{thm:reg_seq_part_of_sys_param}) and the fact that the minimal number of generators for $\mathfrak{m}$ is at least $\dim R$, which is Lemma \ref{lem:reg_maximal_dim_generators}.
nodes.statement_short: Forward via BH 2.2.4; reverse via BH 1.2.12 and the generator bound $\nu(\mathfrak{m})\ge\dim R$.

nodes.name: Standing ring assumption
nodes.statement: All rings are assumed to be unital, commutative and Noetherian without specify.

nodes.name: depth
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $A$-module, $I \subset A$ an ideal, The depth of $M$ with respect to $I$, denoted $\depth_I M$, is the supremum of the length of $M$-regular sequences contained in $I$ (so $IM \neq M$ it's weakly regular), or $\infty$ otherwise. If $A$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak{m}$, denote $\depth M := \depth_\mathfrak{m}M$.
nodes.statement_short: $\depth_I M$ is the sup of lengths of $M$-regular sequences in $I$; for local $A$, $\depth M=\depth_{\mathfrak{m}}M$.
nodes.label: def:depth

nodes.name: Regular sequences extend to systems of parameters
nodes.statement: Any regular sequence is part of a system of parameters
conclusions: Any regular sequence is part of a system of parameters
nodes.label: thm:reg_seq_part_of_sys_param

nodes.name: Proof of BH 1.2.12
nodes.statement: This is from BH chapter 1, and uses associated primes. It also uses the definition of dimension of a module, Let \(x \in \mathfrak{m}\) an \(M\)-regular element. As \(x \in R\) is \(M\)-regular, it is not in any associated prime (Lemma \ref{lem:assoc_prime_zero_divisor}). Then, as the associated primes are minimal among the primes that contain the annihilator (which is the support), we have that the previous statement implies that \[ \dim M / xM \leq \dim M - 1 \] by corollary \ref{cor:quotient_non_minimal_sub_dim_1} By dimension theory (see BH A.4), this inequality is an equality. Given a regular sequence, iterate this process. Once we get to the end of this process, we can extend this sequence (by prime avoidance?) to a sequence of \(\dim M\) elements, by definition (of system of parameters) we have a system of parameters for M.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate: each regular element avoids associated primes and drops dimension by exactly one; then extend to $\dim M$ elements.

nodes.name: Koszul complex
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a (Noetherian?) ring, $M$ be an (finitely generated?) $R$-module and $a \in M$. Then for each graded component in $\bigwedge_R M$ there is a restriction of $R$-linear map $d_a := \underline{\ } \wedge a: \bigwedge_R M \to \bigwedge_R M$: $$d_i: \bigwedge_R^i M \to \bigwedge_R^{n+1}M \text{ where } x \mapsto x \wedge a \text{ for all } x \in \bigwedge_{R}^i M$$ So that $d_a = \bigoplus_{i \in \mathbb{Z}}d_i$, the \textbf{Koszul complex} is then the cochain complex $$\begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow[r] & \bigwedge^{0}_R M \arrow[r, "d_{0}"] & \bigwedge^1_R M \arrow[r, "d_1"] & \dots \bigwedge_R^i M\arrow[r, "d_i"] & \bigwedge_R^{i+1} M \arrow[r] & \dots \end{tikzcd}$$ It's indeed a complex as $d_a^2 = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Koszul complex of $a\in M$: the exterior algebra $\bigwedge_R M$ with differential $x\mapsto x\wedge a$.
nodes.label: def:KoszulComplex

nodes.name: Dual Koszul Complex
nodes.statement: The chain complex dual to koszul complex via the functor $\operatorname{Hom}(-,R)$ .
nodes.label: def:DualKoszulComplex

nodes.name: Koszul Complex is Self-Dual
nodes.statement: If $M \cong R^m$ is a free $R$-module, then applying the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Hom}_R(\ , R)$ gives us an isomorphic chain complex $$K_{\bullet}(a) :\begin{tikzcd} \bigwedge^{i+1}_R R^m \arrow[r, "d_{i+1}"] & \bigwedge^i_R R^m \arrow[r, "d_i"] & \bigwedge^{i-1}_R R^m \arrow[r] & \dots R^m \arrow[r, "d_1"] & R \arrow[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd}$$
assumptions: $M \cong R^m$ is a free $R$-module
conclusions: applying the contravariant functor $\operatorname{Hom}_R(\ , R)$ gives us an isomorphic chain complex
nodes.statement_short: For free $M=R^m$, the $R$-dual of the Koszul complex is isomorphic to the Koszul chain complex.
nodes.label: prop:free_koszul_is_iso_to_dual

nodes.name: Differential of DualKoszul
nodes.statement: Taking $\{e_1, \dots, e_m\}$ as the standard basis of $R^m$, we may write the differential of DualKoszul $K(a_1, \dots, a_m)$ as: $$\bigwedge^{i+1}_R R^m \to \bigwedge^i_R R^m: \wedge \dots \wedge e_{j_{i+1}} \mapsto \sum_{k=1}^{i+1} (-1)^{i+k} a_{j_k} e_{j_{1}} \wedge \dots \wedge \widehat{e_{j_k}} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{j_{i+1}}$$ Where $\widehat{e_{j_k}}$ means the $j_k$-th term is removed, so that the image is in $\bigwedge^{i} R^m$.
nodes.statement_short: Explicit alternating-sum formula for the dual Koszul differential on the standard basis wedges.
nodes.label: prop:diff_of_dual_koszul

nodes.name: tensor product of chain complexes
nodes.statement: Let $K, L$ be two chain complexes, the tensor product of $K$ and $L$, denoted as $K \otimes L$ is defined to be the chain complex $$(K \otimes L)_r := \bigoplus_{p + q = r}K_p \otimes_R L_q$$ Where the differential is defined as $d = (-1)^q d_K + d_L$.
nodes.statement_short: $(K\otimes L)_r=\bigoplus_{p+q=r}K_p\otimes L_q$ with signed differential.
nodes.label: def:complex_tensor_product

nodes.name: Koszul complex of one element exact iff regular
nodes.statement: $K(x)$ is exact exept for the rightmost side iff $x$ is regular.
conclusions: $K(x)$ is exact exept for the rightmost side iff $x$ is regular.
equivalent_conditions: $K(x)$ is exact exept for the rightmost side
nodes.label: lem:koszul_of_length_2

nodes.name: Tensor with K(x) as a mapping cone
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a bounded below complex of $R$-modules, and $x \in R$, then $$(L \otimes K(x))_i \cong L_i \oplus L_{i-1}$$ Where $d_i: (L_i \oplus L_{i-1}) \to (L_{i-1}\oplus L_{i-2})$ is given by the matrix $$d_i = \begin{pmatrix}d_L & (-1)^i \cdot x \\ 0 & d_L\end{pmatrix}$$
assumptions: Let $L$ be a bounded below complex of $R$-modules, and $x \in R$
conclusions: $$(L \otimes K(x))_i \cong L_i \oplus L_{i-1}$$
nodes.statement_short: $L\otimes K(x)$ is the mapping cone of multiplication by $x$ on $L$.
nodes.label: lem:koszul_tensor_as_mapping_cone

nodes.name: Koszul complex as a tensor product
nodes.statement: Let $(a_1, \dots, a_n) \in R^n$ then: $$K(a_1, \dots, a_n) \cong K(a_1) \otimes \dots \otimes K(a_n)$$
assumptions: Let $(a_1, \dots, a_n) \in R^n$
conclusions: $$K(a_1, \dots, a_n) \cong K(a_1) \otimes \dots \otimes K(a_n)$$
nodes.label: thm:long_koszul_build_by_tensoring

nodes.name: Long exact sequence of Koszul homology
nodes.statement: Let $L$ be a complex of $R$-modules, then there is a long exact sequence \[\begin{tikzcd} \dots & {H_i(L)} & {H_i(L)} & {H_i(L\otimes K(a))} & {H_{i-1}(L)} & \dots \arrow[from=1-1, to=1-2] \arrow["{\cdot a}", from=1-2, to=1-3] \arrow[from=1-3, to=1-4] \arrow[from=1-4, to=1-5] \arrow[from=1-5, to=1-6] \end{tikzcd}\] \begin{proof} $L \otimes K(a)$ is in exactly the mapping cone. \end{proof}
assumptions: Let $L$ be a complex of $R$-modules
conclusions: there is a long exact sequence
nodes.statement_short: Long exact sequence $H_i(L)\xrightarrow{a}H_i(L)\to H_i(L\otimes K(a))\to H_{i-1}(L)$.
nodes.label: lem:koszul_induces_long_exact_seq

nodes.name: Proof of the Koszul long exact sequence
nodes.statement: $L \otimes K(a)$ is in exactly the mapping cone.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $L\otimes K(a)$ with the mapping cone.

nodes.name: Long exact sequence for adding one element
nodes.statement: Denote $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ and $a' = (a_1, \dots, a_{n+1})$ then there is a long exact sequence: \[\begin{tikzcd} {H_i(K(a) \otimes M)} & {H_i(K(a) \otimes M)} & {H_i(K(a') \otimes M)} & {H_{i-1}(K(a) \otimes M)} & \arrow[shorten <=8pt, from=1-1, to=1-2] \arrow[shorten <=8pt, "{\cdot a_{n+1}}", from=1-2, to=1-3] \arrow[shorten <=8pt, from=1-3, to=1-4] \arrow[shorten <=8pt, from=1-4, to=1-5] \end{tikzcd}\]
nodes.statement_short: Long exact sequence relating Koszul homology of $a$ and $a'=(a,a_{n+1})$ with $M$.
nodes.label: cor:tensor_koszul_induced_long_exact_seq

nodes.name: Weakly regular sequences have acyclic Koszul homology
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module, and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a weakly $M$-regular sequence. Then $H_i(K(a) \otimes M) = 0$ for all $i > 0$.
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $R$-module, and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a weakly $M$-regular sequence.
conclusions: Then $H_i(K(a) \otimes M) = 0$ for all $i > 0$.
nodes.label: thm:reg_seq_implies_koszul_exact

nodes.name: Vanishing H_1 implies regularity in the Jacobson radical
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a sequence in the Jacobson radical $J$ of $R$. If $H_1(K(a) \otimes M) = 0$, then $a$ is $M$-regular.
assumptions: $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module and $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ be a sequence in the Jacobson radical $J$ of $R$
$H_1(K(a) \otimes M) = 0$
conclusions: $a$ is $M$-regular
nodes.label: lem:reg_in_jrad_iff_koszul_exact_at_one

nodes.name: Permutations of regular sequences in the Jacobson radical
nodes.statement: If $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ is an $M$-sequence in the Jacobson radical, so is every permuations of $a$.
assumptions: $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ is an $M$-sequence in the Jacobson radical
conclusions: so is every permuations of $a$
nodes.label: cor:perm_of_reg_seq_in_jrad_is_reg

nodes.name: Tor computes Koszul homology
nodes.statement: $$H_i(K(a) \otimes M) \cong \tor_i^R (R/(a), M)$$
conclusions: $$H_i(K(a) \otimes M) \cong \tor_i^R (R/(a), M)$$
nodes.label: lem:tor_measures_koszul_homology

nodes.name: Koszul homology measures depth
nodes.statement: Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ and $I = \la a_1, \dots, a_n\ra$ then $$\depth_I(M) = n - \max\{i \mid H_i(K(a) \otimes M) \neq 0\}$$
assumptions: Let $a = (a_1, \dots, a_n)$ and $I = \la a_1, \dots, a_n\ra$
conclusions: $$\depth_I(M) = n - \max\{i \mid H_i(K(a) \otimes M) \neq 0\}$$
nodes.label: lem:koszul_homology_mesures_depth

nodes.name: Tor with the residue field and projective dimension
nodes.statement: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m}, k)$ be a local ring, then $$\tor_i^R(k, M) = \pd M$$
assumptions: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m}, k)$ be a local ring
conclusions: $$\tor_i^R(k, M) = \pd M$$
nodes.label: lem:tor_eq_pd_if_local

nodes.name: Projective dimension of a syzygy
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module such that $\pd M < \infty$, let $P$ be a projective module such that $\varphi: P \to M$ is surjective. Then let $K = \ker \varphi$ then either $K$ and $M$ are projecive or $$\pd K = \pd M - 1$$
assumptions: Let $M$ be an $R$-module such that $\pd M < \infty$, let $P$ be a projective module such that $\varphi: P \to M$ is surjective.
conclusions: either $K$ and $M$ are projecive or $$\pd K = \pd M - 1$$
nodes.label: lem:projdim_ker_eq_one_less

nodes.name: Auslander-Buchsbaum formula
nodes.statement: (Auslander-Buchsbaum formula) Let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be a local ring, and $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module, then: $$\pd M = \depth R - \depth M$$
assumptions: Let $(R, \mathfrak{m})$ be a local ring, and $M$ is a finitely generated $R$-module
conclusions: $$\pd M = \depth R - \depth M$$
nodes.label: thm:auslander_buchsbaum_formula

nodes.name: Height bounds length of contained regular sequences
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring and an ideal $I$ conains a regular sequence $a_1, \dots, a_n$, then $\height I \geq n$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring and an ideal $I$ conains a regular sequence $a_1, \dots, a_n$
conclusions: $\height I \geq n$
nodes.label: lem:depth_leq_ht

nodes.name: Height equals depth for ideals generated by regular sequences
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a Noetherian local ring and an ideal $I$ is generated by a regular sequence, then $\height I = \depth_I A = n$.
assumptions: Let $R$ be a Noetherian local ring and an ideal $I$ is generated by a regular sequence
conclusions: $\height I = \depth_I A = n$
nodes.label: lem:depth_eq_ht_if_gen

nodes.name: Koszul complex resolves the residue field
nodes.statement: If $a_1, \dots, a_n$ is a regular sequence in $(R, \mathfrak{m})$, then the Koszul complex $K(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ is a minimal free resolution of $k = R/(a_1, \dots, a_n)$.
assumptions: $a_1, \dots, a_n$ is a regular sequence in $(R, \mathfrak{m})$
conclusions: the Koszul complex $K(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ is a minimal free resolution of $k = R/(a_1, \dots, a_n)$
nodes.label: cor:koszul_min_resl_residue_iff_reg

nodes.name: Auslander-Buchsbaum-Serre Theorem
nodes.statement: (Auslander-Buchsbaums-Serre) A local ring $R$ has finite global dimension iff it's regular.
assumptions: A local ring $R$
conclusions: has finite global dimension iff it's regular
nodes.label: thm:loc_ring_reg_iff_fin_globdim

nodes.name: Alternating multilinear maps are skew-symmetric
nodes.statement: Should be AlternatingMap.map\_perm in mathlib
nodes.label: lem:alternating_multilinear_is_skew_symmetric

nodes.name: Skew-symmetry criterion
nodes.statement: Corollary 2.9

nodes.name: Elementary wedges span the exterior power
nodes.statement: The set $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} : 1 \leq i_1 < \dots i_k \leq d\}$ spans $\bigwedge^k M$.
conclusions: The set $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} : 1 \leq i_1 < \dots i_k \leq d\}$ spans $\bigwedge^k M$.
nodes.label: lem:spans_exterior_power

nodes.name: Antisymmetrization map is alternating
nodes.statement: For $k \geq 1$, the function $M^k \to M^{\otimes k}$ given by \[(m_1, \dots, m_k) \mapsto \sum_{\sigma \in S_k}^{} (\operatorname{sign} \sigma) m_{\sigma(1)} \otimes \dots \otimes m_{\sigma(k)} \] is multilinear and alterating.
assumptions: For $k \geq 1$
conclusions: is multilinear and alterating
nodes.label: lem:multilinear_to_tensor_is_alternating

nodes.name: Exterior power embeds in tensor power
nodes.statement: $\bigwedge^k M \to M^{\otimes k}$ has trivial kernel.
conclusions: $\bigwedge^k M \to M^{\otimes k}$ has trivial kernel.
nodes.label: lem:hom_exterior_power_to_tensor_inj

nodes.name: Elementary wedges are linearly independent
nodes.statement: The set $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} : 1 \leq i_1 < \dots i_k \leq d\}$ is linearly independent in $\bigwedge^k M$.
conclusions: The set $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} : 1 \leq i_1 < \dots i_k \leq d\}$ is linearly independent in $\bigwedge^k M$.
nodes.label: lem:lin_indep_exterior_power

nodes.name: Basis of the exterior power of a finite free module
nodes.statement: If $M$ is a finite free module of rank $d$ and $k \leq d$ then $\bigwedge^k M$ is free of rank $\binom{d}{k}$: for a basis $e_1, \dots, e_d$ of $M$, the $\binom{d}{k}$ elementary wedge products \[ e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} : 1 \leq i_1 < \dots i_k \leq d \] are a basis of $\bigwedge^k M$.
assumptions: $M$ is a finite free module of rank $d$ and $k \leq d$
conclusions: $\bigwedge^k M$ is free of rank $\binom{d}{k}$
the $\binom{d}{k}$ elementary wedge products \[ e_{i_1} \wedge \dots \wedge e_{i_k} : 1 \leq i_1 < \dots i_k \leq d \] are a basis of $\bigwedge^k M$
nodes.label: thm:exterior_power_basis_if_finite_free_module

nodes.name: Strategy: successive prime avoidance
nodes.statement: We will successively apply prime avoidance.
nodes.statement_short: Strategy: successive prime avoidance

nodes.name: Base case: find $x_1$ with $(x_1)$ of height 1
nodes.statement: Base case: \(I\) is not contained in any minimal prime of \(R\), otherwise \(I\) would have height zero (if I had height zero, we're already done). By prime avoidance, we can pick an element \(x_{1}\) which is not in any minimal prime. Thus, any prime containing \(x_{1}\) must also contain a minimal prime, so all such primes have height at least 1. Pick a prime which is minimal among those containing \((x_{1})\) (equivalently, pick one which is minimal in the ring \(R / (x_{1})\)). By the above discussion, it must have height at least one. By Krull's principal ideal/height theorem, it must have at most height 1, and we conclude it has height 1.
nodes.statement_short: Base case: find $x_1$ with $(x_1)$ of height 1

nodes.name: Inductive step: repeat with indices shifted
nodes.statement: Inductive step: Copy-paste the previous discussion, with "zero" replaced by "\(n-1\)", "1" replaced by "\(n\)", and "minimal prime of \(R\) " replaced by "minimal prime containing \((x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i-1})\)", "\(x_{1}\)" replaced by "\(x_{i}\)", and "\((x_{1})\) replaced by \((x_{1}, \ldots, x_{i})\)".
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: repeat with indices shifted

nodes.name: Prime avoidance gives $x_1$ outside all minimal primes
nodes.statement: Base case: \(I\) is not contained in any minimal prime of \(R\), otherwise \(I\) would have height zero (if I had height zero, we're already done). By prime avoidance, we can pick an element \(x_{1}\) which is not in any minimal prime. Thus, any prime containing \(x_{1}\) must also contain a minimal prime, so all such primes have height at least 1.
nodes.statement_short: Prime avoidance gives $x_1$ outside all minimal primes

nodes.name: Krull's theorem bounds the height by 1, so it equals 1
nodes.statement: Pick a prime which is minimal among those containing \((x_{1})\) (equivalently, pick one which is minimal in the ring \(R / (x_{1})\)). By the above discussion, it must have height at least one. By Krull's principal ideal/height theorem, it must have at most height 1, and we conclude it has height 1.
nodes.statement_short: Krull's theorem bounds the height by 1, so it equals 1

nodes.name: Regular element avoids associated primes
nodes.statement: As \(x\) is \(M\)-regular, we have that \(x \notin \mathfrak{p}\) for all \(p \in \operatorname{Assoc} M\), otherwise there would be \(M\)-torsion.
nodes.statement_short: Regular element avoids associated primes

nodes.name: Reduce to $R/\operatorname{Ann}M$, where $x$ avoids minimal primes
nodes.statement: By definition, \(\dim M = \dim R / \operatorname{Ann} M\). The associated primes of \(M\) are the same as the minimal primes in \(R / \operatorname{Ann} M\), so \(x\) is not contained in any such prime.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $R/\operatorname{Ann}M$, where $x$ avoids minimal primes

nodes.name: Lift prime chains and extend by a minimal prime
nodes.statement: But then, any chain of prime ideals in \((R / \operatorname{Ann} M) / (x)\) lifts to a chain in \(R / \operatorname{Ann} M\) of ideals which contain \((x)\). But then the smallest ideal in the chain is not minimal since it contains \(x\), so we can extend it to a minimal prime.
nodes.statement_short: Lift prime chains and extend by a minimal prime

nodes.statement: By dimension theory (see BH A.4), this inequality is an equality.

nodes.statement: Given a regular sequence, iterate this process. Once we get to the end of this process, we can extend this sequence (by prime avoidance?) to a sequence of \(\dim M\) elements, by definition (of system of parameters) we have a system of parameters for M.
